clue.text: Man's main town house — he lived at No 10

parts.note: Douglas is the capital of the Isle of Man
a house is a home

explanation.surface: A man's grand townhouse is described, then we learn its owner once lived in Downing Street.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man' is the Isle of Man, not a person. Sir Alec Douglas-Home was British Prime Minister in 1963-64; No 10 Downing Street is the Prime Minister's official residence.
explanation.definitionFit: Douglas-Home served as Prime Minister, so he resided at Number 10 Downing Street.

clue.text: Model scene in play concealing bits of information

indicators.note: to conceal something is to hold it hidden inside, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: a play is a drama
binary bits are 1 and 0, written here as the look-alike letters I and O

explanation.surface: A stage play hides small facts within a model scene on set.
explanation.walkthrough: Computer bits are ones and zeros, which look like the letters I and O.
explanation.definitionFit: A diorama is a three-dimensional model representing a scene, often in a museum display.

clue.text: Leader of unbelievers locks up a biblical figure

indicators.note: the leader of a group is the one at the front, so take the opening letter

parts.note: first letter of unbelievers

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading from bottom to top, so backwards

parts.note: locks of hair

explanation.surface: The chief of the unbelievers imprisons a figure from the Bible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Locks up' looks like imprisoning; split it, locks is the hair and up turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: Uriah the Hittite is the Old Testament soldier whose wife Bathsheba King David took.

clue.text: Clear Paris Match articles involving British territory

indicators.note: to involve something is to take it in, so the territory sits within the articles

parts.note: LE is a French definite article
Gib is short for Gibraltar, a British overseas territory
a second French article, the plural of the clue word supplying both

explanation.surface: Pieces in the French magazine Paris Match deal with a British territory.
explanation.walkthrough: Paris Match is a French magazine, but here it just signals French; two French articles LE surround GIB.
explanation.definitionFit: Legible writing is clear enough to be read easily.

clue.text: Mystery man, a bit vain — one mischievously turning up

indicators.note: in a down entry, turning upward means the letters run backwards
a bit of the following words means just a stretch of their letters is used

parts.note: the letters run across vaiN ONE MISchievously

explanation.surface: A rather vain mystery man is someone who appears mischievously.
explanation.walkthrough: Read backwards, the letters within 'vain one mis-' spell the author: Georges Simenon, creator of the detective Maigret.
explanation.definitionFit: Simenon wrote the Maigret crime novels, so he is a mystery writer, a man of mystery fiction.

clue.text: Trick shot in golf? Tell me all

parts.note: to trick someone is to outwit them
a golf stroke is a hit, the question mark flagging an example

explanation.surface: Someone asks about a clever golf trick shot, then demands the full story.
explanation.walkthrough: The trick shot is a red herring; Trick and shot are separate words that run together.
explanation.definitionFit: "Out with it!" is an idiom urging someone to speak up and reveal everything.

clue.text: Pie concocted with grouse and bit of fruit peel

indicators.note: something concocted is mixed up from ingredients, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
to grouse is to complain, or carp

explanation.surface: A pie is cooked up with game birds and a bit of fruit peel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grouse' looks like the game bird in a pie; it is the verb to complain.
explanation.definitionFit: The epicarp is the botanical name for the outermost skin layer of a fruit.

clue.text: Loud noise of farm animals running

parts.note: F is forte, the musical direction for loud
lowing is the mooing of cattle

explanation.surface: Noisy cattle running across a farm.
explanation.definitionFit: Water that is running is flowing, a direct synonym for moving liquid.

clue.text: Perhaps I press on, with rift developing

indicators.note: something developing changes form, so the letters take a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone resolves to carry on despite a growing rift.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I' looks like part of the surface sentence, the speaker; it is the definition, with 'Perhaps' signalling an example.
explanation.definitionFit: In grammar, the pronoun I is the first person singular, so I is an example of it.

clue.text: Providing coverage of races in sporting publication

indicators.note: sporting something means wearing or carrying it, so one piece goes about the other

parts.note: MAG is short for magazine
the TT (Tourist Trophy) races are held on the Isle of Man
taken as written

explanation.surface: A sports magazine covers the races.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sporting publication' reads as a sports paper; sporting is the wrapping signal, meaning wearing. The TT races are the Isle of Man motorcycle races.
explanation.definitionFit: Matting covers a floor, so laying it provides a covering.

clue.text: Good film with great start

parts.note: G is the abbreviation for good
E.T. is Spielberg's 1982 film
cracking is informal British for excellent

explanation.surface: A good film that opens with a great beginning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Great start' looks like a single phrase; great is the wordplay and start alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To get cracking is an idiom meaning to begin working without delay.

clue.text: Drug-smuggling arch criminal gets stretch

indicators.note: smuggling something means carrying it hidden inside
criminal suggests something crooked or bent, so the letters are twisted out of order

parts.note: taken as written
E is ecstasy

explanation.surface: An arch-criminal smuggling drugs is given a prison stretch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arch criminal' reads as master villain and 'stretch' as a jail term; arch is the fodder and stretch the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To reach is to stretch out an arm or extend to a point.

clue.text: One wanting good fare from German city keeping up with Turkey's capital

indicators.note: a capital letter is the first one, so the country contributes only its opening letter
keeping something means holding it within

parts.note: Bonn, the former West German capital
viva means long live, the cry of 'up with' someone
first letter of Turkey

explanation.surface: Someone after good food travels from a German city to Ankara.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turkey's capital' suggests Ankara; it is just T, the first letter. Bonn keeps VIVA inside before T is added.
explanation.definitionFit: A bon vivant enjoys a sociable, luxurious life with fine food and drink.

clue.text: Cash allocation farm invested in banks in Tennessee

indicators.note: money invested in something is put inside it
banks are the edges of a river, so take the outside letters

parts.note: the first and last letters of Tennessee
a ranch is a large farm

explanation.surface: Money for a farm is invested in Tennessee banks.
explanation.walkthrough: The financial words 'invested' and 'banks' set a money scene; banks means the edges of Tennessee.
explanation.definitionFit: A tranche is a portion of money released as one instalment of a larger sum.

clue.text: Heard superfans of activity with knights and horses

indicators.note: what is heard is a matter of sound, not spelling

parts.note: chess uses knights, and nuts are fanatics

explanation.surface: Fanatics of an activity involving knights and horses, such as jousting.
explanation.walkthrough: Knights and horses suggest medieval jousting; the knights are chess pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A chestnut is a reddish-brown horse, so chestnuts are horses of that colour.

clue.text: Pathetic sort of mobile phone cover for owner

indicators.note: mobile means able to move, so these letters move into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: a cover is the outside of something, so take the outer letters

parts.note: the first and last letters of owner

explanation.surface: A sad sort of mobile phone case for its owner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mobile phone cover' reads as a phone case; mobile rearranges phone, and cover takes the edges of owner.
explanation.definitionFit: A no-hoper is a person with no prospect of success, a pathetic or useless type.

clue.text: Close to collapse, a short nap is most relaxing

indicators.note: short means cut off, so the last letter goes
the close of a word is its end, so take its final letter

parts.note: last letter of collapse
taken as written
a siesta is an afternoon nap

explanation.surface: When near collapse, a brief nap is the most relaxing thing.
explanation.definitionFit: Easiest is the superlative of easy, meaning least tense or most at ease.

clue.text: Gambler's odds on gold getting smuggled in pouch

parts.note: SP is starting price, the odds at the start of a race
OR is gold in heraldry
to run goods is to smuggle them, so ran means smuggled

explanation.surface: A gambler's odds-on bet on gold being smuggled inside a pouch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smuggled in' looks like a container signal, but to run goods (as in gun-running) is to smuggle them, and 'in' just links to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A sporran is the pouch worn at the front of a Scottish kilt.

clue.text: Not lying about Germany to the French PM

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece surrounds the other

parts.note: what is not a lie is true
D is the international vehicle code for Germany
au is French for 'to the'

explanation.surface: A truthful statement about Germany made to the French Prime Minister.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The French PM' tempts a solver toward a French leader; 'to the French' is wordplay, and the PM is Canadian.
explanation.definitionFit: Pierre and Justin Trudeau both served as Prime Minister of Canada.

clue.text: Like a fiend's appeal over attending prison briefly

parts.note: SA is sex appeal

indicators.note: turned over means flipped round, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: to be at something is to attend it

indicators.note: briefly means cut short, so the word loses its last letter

parts.note: the nick is British slang for prison

explanation.surface: Describing the allure of a devil who is briefly in jail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Like a fiend's' is adjectival, describing what belongs to a fiend.
explanation.definitionFit: Satanic means devilish, pertaining to Satan, the archfiend.

clue.text: Compilers upset while away in bar temporarily

indicators.note: upset means turned upside down, which in a down entry flips the letters

parts.note: the setter speaking as 'us'
to while away time is to spend it

explanation.surface: Puzzle setters are distressed while they are away in a pub for a while.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bar' looks like a pub; it is the verb meaning to ban.
explanation.definitionFit: To suspend someone is to ban them for a period, debarring them temporarily.

clue.text: Book Vauxhall to cover short distance

indicators.note: covering something means wrapping around it

parts.note: the Nova was a Vauxhall car model
an ell is an old unit of length

explanation.surface: Reserve a Vauxhall car for a brief journey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Book' looks like a verb, to reserve the car; it is the noun. Vauxhall is a British car maker.
explanation.definitionFit: A novella is a short novel, a type of book.

clue.text: Series of penalties drive away solicitors

parts.note: to shoo is to drive away
touts solicit custom

explanation.surface: Penalty after penalty drives the lawyers off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Solicitors' suggests lawyers; here they are people soliciting business.
explanation.definitionFit: Shoot-outs are penalty contests deciding drawn football matches, plural matching 'Series'.

clue.text: Section of poetry in French, mostly empty

indicators.note: mostly means not all of it, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: en is French for in
void means empty

explanation.surface: A passage of French poetry that is largely empty.
explanation.definitionFit: An envoi is the short closing stanza of a ballade, a section of a poem.

clue.text: Rolls with eggs on the outside — flipping silly idea!

indicators.note: flipping something turns it over, so the result reads backwards
lying on the outside means wrapping around something

parts.note: roe is fish eggs
RR stands for Rolls-Royce

explanation.surface: Bread rolls with eggs on top: what a stupid idea!
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rolls' looks like bread; it is the car maker. 'Flipping' doubles as a mild British curse.
explanation.definitionFit: An error is a mistake, a wrong or foolish belief.

clue.text: Take care of U-turn when travelling about

indicators.note: travelling letters move around, so they arrive in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
re means concerning, about

explanation.surface: Be careful making a U-turn while driving around.
explanation.definitionFit: To nurture is to care for and encourage the growth of someone.

clue.text: US lawman left case of unnerving obstruction of hearing

parts.note: Wyatt Earp, the Wild West marshal
L for left

indicators.note: a case is the outer shell, so only the outside letters count

parts.note: the first and last letters of unnerving

explanation.surface: A US marshal left an unnerving case of obstructing a court hearing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Obstruction of hearing' sounds legal after a lawman and a case; it is literal.
explanation.definitionFit: An earplug is inserted in the ear to block sound, literally obstructing the hearing.

clue.text: Send us wild in Italian opera? This might!

definitions.text: Send us wild in Italian opera? This might!

indicators.note: in places one piece within the other

parts.note: Norma is Bellini's Italian opera

indicators.note: running wild means out of control, so the letters are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Which Italian opera aria could drive us wild? This one!
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition: Nessun Dorma, the Puccini aria from Turandot famously sung by Pavarotti, drives audiences wild.
explanation.definitionFit: Nessun Dorma is a rousing tenor aria from an Italian opera, able to thrill a crowd.
